textbookText: i. They have boat shaped or streamlined body without any projections from body that resist flying. ii. In bat, sustaining organs are called patagia which are paper-thin, elastic extensions of leathery skin from the lateral sides of body, legs and tail. iii. In birds, sustaining organs are wings which are modified fore limbs with powerful flight muscles and feathers. iv. Body is covered by various types of feather like quills, contour feather, down feather which keep them light, smooth and well protected from adverse environmental condition. v. They have light and spongy bones, also called pneumatic bones. vi. Lungs are connected with air sacs for providing sufficient oxygen to tissues for the continuous liberation of energy during flight. vii. They have keeled sternum which facilitate passing in air and also serve as the site for the attachment of flight muscle (pectoral muscle) of wing. viii. Birds have developed special mechanism by their leg muscles and tendons to grip or perch on the tree branches, electrical wires, rod etc while resting. This is called perching. ix. Other adaptational features in them are body weight reduced, internal structure are centralized, absence of left ovary, absence of urinary bladder, fused vertebrae etc. also aid in flying.

Figure: 9.1.7 Air sac with lungs in birds Figure: 9.1.8 Perching in bird 2. Passive flight In passive flight, animals fly in air for short duration and cover only few meter horizontal distances. Animals leap or jump from certain height i.e. from top of tree, Biology, Grade 11 | 438

hills, buildings etc. and later come down to the earth by gravity in the short time. At this moment, they cover some horizontal distance with the help of sustaining organ or patagia. This adaptation is also called Gliding adaptation. Animals which glide in air are flying fish (Exocoetus), Flying frog (Rhacophorus), Draco (flying lizard), flying snake (chrysopelea), flying lemur (Cynocephalus) etc.

Adaptational features include: i. They have developed patagia, a fold of skin stretched on the either lateral side of between trunk and limbs. ii. In flying fish, pectoral fins are extended as patagia and their caudal fin is hypobatic (ventral lobe larger for quick take off from water surface). iii. Patagia are supported by about 7 pair of elongated ribs (in Draco).

Figure: 9.1.9 Aerial adaptation: passive flight iv. In flying snake, ribs are spread, ventral body surface is made flat and concave while gliding. v. Some frogs glide in air with the help of their webbed toes. The toes are also provided with adhesive pad for safe landing after the glide is over.
